message.content:
The exact number of distinct legal positions that can arise in a game of chess is astronomically large – on the order of **10^43 to 10^50**.  This estimate is often called the *Shannon number* (after Claude Shannon), and it represents a lower bound on the true count.  More recent computational work has pushed the estimate up to roughly **10^46** legal positions.

If you’re asking about the number of possible *games* (i.e., sequences of moves from the starting position to any terminal position), the figure is even larger – about **10^120** distinct games.  This is sometimes called the *game-tree complexity* of chess.

So, in short:

| Quantity | Rough estimate |
|----------|----------------|
| Legal positions | ~10^43–10^50 (≈10^46) |
| Possible games | ~10^120 |

These numbers illustrate why exhaustive search of the entire game tree is infeasible, and why modern chess engines rely on heuristics, pruning, and evaluation functions.
